source_text: CAPUT QUARTUM, De unitate Dei, ubi ostenditur unum esse Deum. Hactenus probavimus esse Deum, & qua via ac virtute eum cognoscamus: nunc eundem unum esse, adversus fictitium deorum numerum demonstrabimus. Est igitur alterum axioma fidei nostrae ASSERTIO: DEUS EST UNUS. Tertullianus adversus Marcionem: Veritas Christiana directe pronunciat, Deus, si non unus est, non est. Unus autem est eo sensu quem Apostolus declarat 1 Cor. 8.4. Et Esa. 44.6; Joh. 17.3 solum verum Deum.
english: CHAPTER FOUR. On the unity of God, where it is shown that God is one.
Thus far we have proved that God is, and by what way and power we may know Him: now we will demonstrate that the same is one, against the fictitious number of gods.

There is therefore another axiom of our faith, the ASSERTION: GOD IS ONE. Tertullian (Against Marcion): Christian truth directly pronounces, God, if He is not one, is not. But He is one in the sense the Apostle declares (1 Corinthians 8:4). And Isaiah 44:6; John 17:3 — the only true God.

source_text: Rufinus in expositione symboli: Deum unum esse non numero, sed universitate: ut unus sol, ita ut alius addi non possit. Multo magis Deus unus non numeri sed universitatis vocabulo nuncupatur, quia alius non sit. Haec Dei unitas Scripturis manifesta est: Deut. 4.35.39; 6.4; Psal. 18.32; Esa. 44-48; Joh. 17.3; Rom. 3.29; 1 Cor. 8.4; Gal. 3.20; Ephes. 4.6; 1 Tim. 2.5. Protervis tamen ingeniis rationibus naturae lumine notis persuadenda est. Non tantum unum esse Deum evincemus, sed nec plures esse posse demonstrabimus.
english: Rufinus in his exposition of the Creed: God is one not by number but by universality — as one sun, so that another cannot be added. Much more is God named one by a word of universality, because there is no other.

This unity of God is manifest in the Scriptures (Deuteronomy 4:35, 39; 6:4; Psalm 18:32; Isaiah 44-48; John 17:3; Romans 3:29; 1 Corinthians 8:4; Galatians 3:20; Ephesians 4:6; 1 Timothy 2:5). Yet to stubborn minds it must be persuaded by reasons known by nature's light. We will not only prove that God is one, but also demonstrate that there cannot be many.

source_text: PRIMA sumitur ab ordine partium universi. Ubi ordo est, unum esse aliquid oportet ad quod cetera reducantur. Aristoteles: Non est bonum pluralitas principatuum: unus princeps esto. Athanasius: Multitudo deorum nullitas est deorum. SECUNDA: Deus summa est unitas, summa veritas, summa bonitas, quae non potest esse nisi unica & pura. TERTIA: si plures dii sint, aut omnino differunt, aut omnino unum sunt, aut partim differunt partim unum: primum absurdum; si alterum, jam non plures sed unus.
english: THE FIRST is taken from the order of the universe's parts. Where there is order, there must be something one to which the rest are reduced. Aristotle: a plurality of rulerships is not good; let there be one ruler. Athanasius: a multitude of gods is a nullity of gods.
THE SECOND: God is highest unity, highest truth, highest goodness, which cannot be except unique and pure.
THE THIRD: if there were many gods, they either differ altogether, or are altogether one, or partly both: the first is absurd; if the second, they were already not many but one.

source_text: QUARTA: aut unus est Deus, aut si plures sint infinitos esse oportet; infiniti autem esse nequeunt. QUINTA est a sapientum omnium unanimi consensu. SEXTA: plurima gentilitiorum deorum nomina unum Deum designant diversis attributis. Jupiter & Pluto, Phoebus, Dionysus unum est. Deus assistat in omnibus unus. Philosophus de mundo ad Alexandrum: Unus Deus cum sit, pluribus nominibus est appellatus.
english: THE FOURTH: either God is one, or if there are many there must be infinitely many; but there cannot be infinitely many.
THE FIFTH is from the unanimous consensus of all the wise.

THE SIXTH: most names of the Gentiles' gods designate one God under diverse attributes. Jupiter and Pluto, Phoebus, Dionysus are one. God stands as one in all. The philosopher On the World to Alexander: though God is one, He is called by many names.

source_text: SEPTIMA est a sensu & confessione vulgi ethnicorum. Orosius: Pagani non se plures deos sequi, sed sub uno Deo magno plures ministros venerari fatentur. Tertullianus Apologet. 17: Anima, quum resipiscit, Deum nominat solum — O testimonium animae naturaliter Christianae! Lactantius: Quum jurant, quum gratias agunt, non Jovem aut deos multos, sed Deum nominant. OCTAVA: nihil est quod deorum multitudini patrocinari queat. Hermes Trismegistus: unus haec omnia praestat. Facit igitur omnia Deus. Hacpropter Deus unitati comparari consuevit.
english: THE SEVENTH is from the sense and confession of the pagan crowd. Orosius: pagans confess that they do not follow many gods, but under one great God venerate many ministers. Tertullian (Apology 17): the soul, when it comes to its senses, names God alone — O testimony of a soul naturally Christian! Lactantius: when they swear or give thanks, they name not Jupiter or many gods but God.
THE EIGHTH: nothing can champion a multitude of gods. Hermes Trismegistus: one performs all these. Therefore God does all things. For this reason God is customarily compared to unity.

source_text: Si malum bono permixtum cum Gnosticis, Manichaeis & Encratitis objicias, quod a bono Deo esse nequit, & alium Deum a quo mala oriantur statuendum colligas: respondemus, 1. mali causam efficientem nullam quaerendam esse, sed deficientem, quae non est Deus, a quo nil nisi bonum esse potest, sed ipsa creatura bonitate sua excidens, quia mali natura consistit in privatione. 2. Si Deus sit malorum causa, erit summum malum; summum malum esse nequit, quia seipsum destruit. 3. Si summum malum est Deus, neque aget, neque cognoscet, neque vivet, neque erit omnino, quia agere, cognoscere, vivere bona sunt.
english: If with the Gnostics, Manichaeans, and Encratites you object that evil mixed with good cannot be from the good God, and gather that another God from whom evils arise must be posited: we answer,

1. that no efficient cause of evil is to be sought, but a deficient one, which is not God — from whom nothing but good can be — but the creature itself falling from its goodness, because evil's nature consists in privation.

2. If God were the cause of evils, He would be the highest evil; but there cannot be a highest evil, because it destroys itself. 3. If this God is the highest evil, He will neither act nor know nor live nor be at all, because to act, to know, and to live are goods.
